---
title: Plugin or pull request?
---

Both routes give a method the same standing, since the built-ins have no privileges.
The difference is where the code lives and who releases it.

Write a plugin when the method

- brings its own heavy dependency, as `laplacekit-transformers` brings `transformers`.
  The defaults never depend on what is installed, so **laplacekit** itself only depends on what its built-ins need.
- is a research method or still experimental, and should move at its own pace, with its own releases.
- fits the existing protocols.
  Everything in these pages can be done from outside the repository.

Send a pull request when

- the method belongs in the built-ins and needs no new dependency, e.g., a simple curvature method that `lk.curvature.default` should be able to pick.
- it fixes a bug in **laplacekit**.
- it needs a change in the core: a new protocol, a new operator pair that the priors and predictives must know, or a new capability in the probe.
  The core is the one part that plugins can't extend, so these always go through a pull request.

## When a plugin becomes first-party

A third-party plugin can become first-party, with an extra (`pip install "laplacekit[mylib]"`) and an alias (`lk.mylib`), when

- it wraps a widely used library, so that many users already hold that library's objects;
- it is small;
- the **laplacekit** author will run its tests in CI.

The code stays a separate package and keeps importing only the public API.
[Overview](overview.qmd) has the full comparison.
